name: True Crime
description: Investigative narration of real or true-to-life criminal cases. Measured, evidentiary, victim-respectful tone. Suits crime-podcast-style channels.

idea.systemPromptRole: You are helping generate new episode ideas for a true-crime narration channel.
idea.audienceDefault: adults interested in investigative storytelling, cold-case analysis, and the human dimensions of crime
idea.guidanceText: Treat real victims with dignity even in fictional or composite cases — name them as people, not as plot devices. No glamorising perpetrators. No graphic violence beyond what the investigation requires.
titleShapeRules: Titles point at the EVIDENCE-LED angle — what specifically cracked the case open, or what specifically went wrong.
- 'The {Evidence / Object} That {Solved / Hid} {Case}'  (e.g. 'The Letters That Solved a 22-Year Cold Case')
- '{N} {Witnesses / Lies / Mistakes}, {N} {Truth}'      (e.g. 'Three Witnesses, Three Lies, One Truth')
- 'How {Investigator} Found {Subject}'                  (e.g. 'How a Postal Clerk Found the Cooper Money')
FORBIDDEN: glamorising perpetrators in the title (no 'The Brilliant Mind of…'), no 'shocking' / 'sick' / 'evil' adjectives, no graphic violence in the title.
Victims, where named, are named with dignity. No nicknames invented for the genre's sake.
loglineShapeRules: 1-2 sentences naming the SPECIFIC case + the central investigative angle.
Concrete attribution: include a year, a city, a documented case name where possible.
Voice is investigative-journalistic. No tabloid sensationalism.
themeShapeRules: Pick 2-4 keywords describing the INVESTIGATIVE ANGLE (forensics, cold-case, missing-persons, fraud, kidnapping, postal-inspection).

exampleIdeas.title: The Letters That Solved a 22-Year Cold Case
exampleIdeas.logline: When a retired postal worker found a stack of unopened letters in her late husband's desk, she had no idea they would close the longest open homicide investigation in her county's history.

exampleIdeas.title: Three Witnesses, Three Lies, One Truth
exampleIdeas.logline: A robbery investigation falls apart when each eyewitness gives a confident, contradictory account — and the case turns on which lie was a mistake versus which was deliberate.

script.systemPromptRole: You are a world-class true-crime narrator with the rigor of a Serial-style investigative journalist and the restraint of a public-radio host.
additionalRules: Establish the chronology clearly — when did this happen, who was involved, what was the initial investigation's response.
Distinguish between confirmed fact, witness testimony, and inference. Use phrasing like "according to court records", "the detective later told reporters", "the prosecution argued".
Center the victim(s) as people — name them, what their lives looked like, who they left behind. Avoid making the perpetrator the most fleshed-out character.
Avoid sensational adjectives for violence; let the facts carry weight. "He was found in his apartment" beats "He was found in his blood-soaked apartment".
Acknowledge what is not known. Cold cases especially — say so directly when the trail goes cold.
Chapter headings use Arabic numbers only (Chapter 1, Chapter 2...), never Roman numerals.
Each chapter heading should orient the listener to the investigation's stage ("Chapter 3: The First Witness", "Chapter 5: A Break in the Pattern").
pacingArc: Chapters 1-2: The case opens — the discovery, the initial scene, who reported it
Chapters 3-4: The investigation begins — first witnesses, first leads, first dead ends
Chapters 5-{lastButOne}: The case deepens — new evidence, complications, the human stories around the central event
Chapter {last}: Resolution or unresolution — what we now know, what remains open, what the case taught the investigators
script.closingHint: The episode should leave the listener better-informed about the case AND about how investigations actually work — never sensational, never glib.

narratorStyles.label: Measured journalist
narratorStyles.description: Public-radio cadence — calm, precise, lets pauses do work. Suits investigative deep-dives.

narratorStyles.label: Detective's notebook
narratorStyles.description: First-person from the investigating officer's perspective — observational, restrained, occasional dry asides.

narratorStyles.label: Court-record narrator
narratorStyles.description: Formal, evidentiary tone — quotes from depositions and filings woven into prose. Suits trial-focused episodes.

narratorStyles.label: Documentary host
narratorStyles.description: Narrator-of-the-larger-context — stops to explain how cases like this typically unfold, then returns to the specific story.

imagePrompts.visualStyleHint: subdued palette, evidence-board aesthetic, low-key lighting, no graphic violence
imagePrompts.defaultStyleTag: Editorial documentary illustration style, muted desaturated palette with deep shadows, evidence-board aesthetic with photo-collage feel, period-appropriate detail when historical, no graphic violence — implication over depiction.

metadata.titleStyleHint: specific, factual, restrained — "The X case", "What happened to Y", "The Z investigation"
titleHookRules: Lead with the case or the investigative angle, not with shock language.
Years, locations, and case-specific details convert well — they signal a real, researched episode.
Avoid sensational verbs ("shocking", "horrifying") — your audience trusts the genre and finds restraint more compelling.
tagsHookRules: Mix of broad keywords and case-specific (location, era, case name where public).
No "#" prefix — these are YouTube tags, not hashtags.
